newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia calls for extension of UN mandate. [CORRECTED 15:37 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia calls for extension of UN mandate. [CORRECTED 15:37 GMT]

text.p: Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic has asked the U.N. Security Council to extend the U.N. mandate in Eastern Slavonia for another six months, Belgrade media reported on Thursday.
Eastern Slavonia, the last Serb enclave in Croatia, is administered by the United Nations, whose current mandate ends on July 15 when the area is due to come under Croatian government control.
However the United States has hinted it might call for the current mandate covering 5,000 troops to be extended unless Croatia urgently improves its treatment of local Serbs.
The UNTAES force should remain in the region until January 15, 1998, Milutinovic said in a letter to the security council, the independent Belgrade news agency Beta reported.
(Corrects attribution from state news agency Tanjug)

Such a decision would be "politically extremely important" not only for the "full and succesful implementation of the basic (Serb-Croat) agreement but also for the "consolidation of peace and strengthening of security in the region", he was quoted as saying.
Eastern Slavonia, together with two other enclaves, was siezed by its Serb minority in 1991 when they revolted against Croatia's secession from federal Yugoslavia.
Croatia recaptured all other Serb-held territory in a lightning offensive in 1995 and Eastern Slavonia is now home to thousands of Serbs who fled their advance.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright put Croatian President Franjo Tudjman publicly to task this weekend over the harassment of Serbs returning to their homes in Croatia in line with the Dayton peace accord.
In an unusually conciliatory speech to Serbs on Monday Tudjman vowed to create conditions for all ethnic minorities to live in peace.
The West and Belgrade fear a flood of refugees once the Croatian authorities establish their rule in an area notorious for atrocities during the bitter six-month war in 1991.
"The extension of the U.N. mandate would be the best signal to one of the signatories (of the agreeement) to change its behaviour," Milutinovic said referring to Croatia.

He said this would force Zagreb to "resolve current problems instead of exerting pressures and making ommissions, especially regarding the security of Serbs in Eastern Slavonia, to prevent their leaving the region."

The Security Council will vote soon on whether the present mandate should be prolonged or reduced to a monitoring mission with fewer troops. Croatia has already agreed that some form of U.N. presence can remain until January next year.
